# What is Kailash {#what-is-kailash}

Kailash OS is a **NixOS-based Linux distribution for security
professionals and AI engineers working on AI-native offence, defence
and platform work** — built declaratively with Nix flakes. It keeps
the integrated experience Kali popularised (curated tools, desktop
menu categories, live images, generated documentation) and re-aims it
at four pillars: **appsec, apisec, mlsec, aisec**.

## Why it exists

Security work on AI systems needs tooling that is:

- **Reproducible** — an experimental result only counts if it can be
  re-run against the same tool versions. Every package is pinned to an
  exact source revision with a content hash; the lockfile is the
  version of the system.
- **Declared, not implied** — the tool catalogue is a single manifest
  that drives packaging, the desktop menu, the CLI, and this guide's
  reference section. Nothing is installed ad hoc; nothing drifts.
- **Safety-aware by construction** — tools that talk to live targets
  or run experimental code are classified and gated, not silently
  enabled (see [Safety classes](../governance/safety-classes.qmd)).

## What it is not

Kailash inherits Kali's shape, not its full inventory. Deliberately
out of scope: no Active Directory / lateral-movement arsenal, no
social-engineering pack, and no wifi/RF/Bluetooth attack tooling —
with one opt-in carve-out: software-defined radio (SDR) is kept
because it is the substrate for signal/voice ML research, not a radio
hacking kit. The classic layer is a smaller, opinionated, software-only
subset of Kali's ~300 tools.

## Who it is for

Practitioners and researchers doing AI security assessment:

- **Red-team work against AI systems** — LLM red teaming (jailbreaks,
  prompt injection, multi-turn attacks), adversarial ML, agentic and
  MCP attack surfaces.
- **Defenders and evaluators** — guardrails, detection and
  observability, assurance/evals, model provenance and signing.
- **Platform engineers** — the MLOps, storage, serving and local
  inference stack that hosts and observes the models under test.

The pairing thesis behind the catalogue: an attack tool is most useful
when the system that observes and defends against it ships alongside
it — the distribution carries both halves of the exercise.
